title: Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
summary: The last capstone applies chapter 9's reverse engineering, chapter 8's debugging and chapter 7's assembly to a program whose source you have not read, and turns the findings into a clear technical report. Targets are chosen so the analysis is legal and checkable: open-source programs you build yourself with the source set aside, practice programs published for analysis, and programs a classmate writes for you. The lesson covers choosing a target, the method, the report's structure and how to check your conclusions against the truth.
markdown:
## Choosing a target The analysis must be **legal** and **checkable**. Good targets: | Target | Why it works | |---|---| | An **open-source program** you compile yourself, in Release, then analyse without reading the source; the source is the answer key afterwards | Legal under its licence; you can check every conclusion | | A **practice program written for analysis** (often called a "crackme" or reversing challenge) from a site whose rules allow it | Made for this; usually comes with write-ups to compare | | A program a **classmate or friend writes for you** with a short brief ("a small file format and a checksum"), who keeps the source until you finish | Realistic and fun; both of you learn | | One of **your own old programs** whose source you no longer remember | Surprisingly instructive | Not suitable: commercial software or games whose licence forbids reverse engineering, anything protected by anti-tamper (lesson 17.06), online games, and anything you would analyse to get around a protection or a payment. Lesson 9.01's ground rules apply unchanged. A good size is 50 to 500 KB of code: large enough to need a method, small enough to finish. A command-line tool with a file format (a compressor, an image converter, a small game with save files) is ideal. ## The method ```mermaid flowchart TB A["1. Triage
PE headers, imports, strings, sections"] --> B["2. Run it
observe files, output, behaviour"] B --> C["3. Find the interesting code
cross-references from strings and imports"] C --> D["4. Understand it
functions, loops, structs, in the disassembler"] D --> E["5. Confirm dynamically
breakpoints, watch memory, change inputs"] E -->|"new question"| C E --> F["6. Document
names, structures, diagrams, the report"] ``` 1. **Triage** (lessons 9.02, 9.03): architecture, sections, imports (file, network, crypto, UI?), exported functions, strings. Write down hypotheses: "it reads `.cfg` files", "it uses zlib". 2. **Run it** in a VM or sandbox folder and watch with Process Monitor: files it opens, registry keys, what it prints. 3. **Find the interesting code** (lesson 9.08): from a string such as `"invalid header"` or an import such as `CreateFileW`, follow cross-references back to the functions that use them. 4. **Understand it** (lessons 9.04 to 9.06, 9.09, chapter 7): rename functions and variables in the disassembler as you go, reconstruct structs from field offsets, recognise loops, switches, vtables and library code. 5. **Confirm dynamically** (lesson 9.07): break on the function, check arguments and results match your reading, change an input byte and predict what happens. 6. **Document**: names, structures and the report below. Keep a **lab notebook**: every address, hypothesis, test and result, dated. It is what turns hours of clicking into a report. ## The report | Section | Contents | |---|---| | **Summary** | What the program does, in one paragraph, for someone who will not read further | | **Target and method** | Exact file, version, hash, how it was obtained and why analysing it is permitted; tools used | | **Architecture** | Main modules or components and how they interact, with a diagram | | **Function map** | A table of the important functions: address, your name, purpose, confidence | | **Data structures** | Reconstructed structs with offsets, sizes and field meanings | | **File format or protocol** | A byte-level description, if the program has one, with an example decoded by hand | | **Findings** | Anything notable: bugs, unsafe patterns (lesson 17.04), surprising design choices | | **Verification** | How each major conclusion was confirmed, and what is still uncertain | | **Comparison** (open-source targets) | What you got right, wrong and missed, once you read the source | The **confidence** column matters: "high (confirmed in the debugger)", "medium (consistent with the code)", "low (a guess from the name of a string)". Honest uncertainty is what makes a report trustworthy. ## Acceptance criteria - The target is one of the permitted kinds, recorded with its hash and licence. - The function map covers the program's main path from `main` (or `WinMain`) to its output, with at least 15 functions named. - At least two structures are reconstructed with every field's offset. - If the program has a file format, a small program of yours reads or writes it correctly (proof of understanding). - Every high-confidence claim has a recorded dynamic confirmation. - For an open-source target, the comparison section is honest about errors. ## Stretch goals - Write a script for your disassembler (Ghidra's Python or Java API) that applies your function names and struct definitions automatically, and include it. - Analyse two builds of the same program (Debug and Release, or two versions) and document what changed. - Turn the report into a short talk for classmates. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Reading everything in order > Start from strings, imports and behaviour, and work towards the interesting code. > [!warning] Not writing things down > Without a notebook, you will analyse the same function twice. > [!warning] Stating guesses as facts > Give every conclusion a confidence and the evidence for it. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Which targets are suitable for this capstone? - Any program you can download, including commercial games + Permitted, checkable programs, such as open source you build - Online games, as long as you do not cheat while playing - Protected software, since protections are the most interesting part > Not commercial software that forbids it, protected or online games, or anything analysed to defeat a protection. Practice programs published for analysis, a classmate's program, and your own old programs also qualify. ? What are the six steps of the method? - Decompile, copy, rename, recompile, test, publish - Read the licence, buy the program, install it, play it, uninstall it, write a review - Patch, run, crash, dump, analyse, repeat + Triage, observe, find code via strings, understand, confirm, document > Confirming dynamically is what turns a reading of the code into a verified claim. ? What makes the report trustworthy? - Its length and the number of screenshots + Recorded permission, a method, verified claims and confidence levels - Using the same words as the program's documentation - Leaving out anything you were unsure about > Saying how confident you are, and why, is more useful to a reader than hiding the uncertain parts. ? Why is an open-source program built yourself a good target? + It is permitted, and the source checks you - Open-source programs have no machine code - It is the only legal target > An answer key, with permission. ? What is the best starting point for finding a program's interesting code? - The first byte of the `.text` section + Strings and imports, then their xrefs - A random function > Work from what you can observe. ? Why does the function map have a confidence column? - To sort the table - It is a legal requirement + To show which claims were confirmed > Honest uncertainty makes a report trustworthy. ```
ideas:
- Pick a small open-source command-line tool, build it in Release with the PDB deleted, and complete steps 1 and 2 of the method.
- Swap brief programs with a classmate and analyse each other's.
- Write the report, then read the source and fill in the comparison section.
